books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage

stimulus.source_note: James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, December 2, 1823; public domain.
stimulus.text: President James Monroe, in his annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823: “...the occasion has been judged proper for asserting, as a principle in which the rights and interests of the United States are involved, that the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers...” He added: “We should consider any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere, as dangerous to our peace and safety.” He added: “With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.”

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, December 2, 1823, public domain
stem: Which of the following best explains the historical situation in which Monroe issued this message?

options.text: Latin American republics had won independence, and the United States feared Europe might help Spain win them back.
The United States had just defeated Britain in the War of 1812 and now ruled Canada as a territory.
options.misconception: The War of 1812 ended in a draw, and Canada stayed British; the United States never ruled it.

options.text: France had just sold Louisiana to the United States, doubling the size of the country overnight.
options.misconception: The Louisiana Purchase happened in 1803, twenty years before Monroe's message.

options.text: The United States had annexed Texas and was already at war with Mexico over its border.
options.misconception: Texas was annexed in 1845 and the Mexican War began in 1846, more than twenty years after 1823.

rationales.A: By 1823 most of Spanish America had broken away from Spain. Background: the United States feared that European powers might help Spain win its colonies back, so Monroe warned them off.
rationales.B: The War of 1812 ended in a draw, and Canada stayed British. The United States never ruled Canada.
rationales.C: The Louisiana Purchase happened in 1803, twenty years before Monroe's message.
rationales.D: Texas was annexed in 1845, and the Mexican War began in 1846, more than twenty years after 1823.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what had just changed in the Americas. Spain's colonies had won independence and become republics.
2. Ask what worried Washington. European powers might help Spain take those republics back.
3. Ask what Monroe could actually do. The United States had a small army and navy, so he issued a warning, not a threat of war.
4. Put it together. The Doctrine spoke boldly because the new republics needed a friend and Europe needed a warning.
Remember: a doctrine can be a bold claim made by a weak power, and still shape a century.
